summary: Describes a protocol that supports 3270 terminal devices more fully than traditional tn3270 practice does, such as device naming and printer support. It is a draft standard.

eli5.summary: Old mainframe computers used special screens. This memo makes it work better to use those screens over the internet.

questions: how does tn3270e negotiate a device name
what is the tn3270e message header
subtitle: A Telnet option that lets clients emulate IBM 3270 terminals and printers, with device names, responses and the ATTN and SYSREQ keys.

tldr.problem: Traditional tn3270 could not emulate 3270 printers, could not ask for a specific device name, did not reliably support ATTN and SYSREQ, and had no SNA response handling or access to Bind information.
tldr.mechanism: TN3270E is a new Telnet option. After agreeing to it, client and server negotiate a device type and name, then a set of functions, and every data message carries a five-byte header.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2355 replaces RFC 1647 and is a Draft Standard that was later updated by RFC 6270. A side that does not want TN3270E can fall back to traditional tn3270.

today: RFC 2355 obsoletes RFC 1647 and is a Draft Standard that was later updated by RFC 6270.

sections.title: Why TN3270E Exists
sections.content:
Traditional tn3270 negotiates three Telnet options (Terminal-Type, Binary Transmission and End of Record) before sending the 3270 data stream. The RFC notes that no RFC specified this as a standard. RFC 1041 tried with the 3270 Regime option, but very few developers and vendors implemented it. The practice is documented in RFC 1576.

The RFC lists shortcomings:

  • No way to emulate 328x class printers.
  • No way to ask for a given device name, which matters because many host applications behave differently by terminal name, and printer emulation absolutely needs it.
  • The ATTN and SYSREQ keys were not universally supported.
  • No SNA positive and negative responses.
  • No way for the client to see the SNA Bind information.
  • No way for a server to learn whether a client supports 3270 structured fields.
sections.eli5: The old way could not say which printer or screen you wanted, and some special keys did not work. TN3270E fixes those gaps.

sections.title: The TN3270E Option
sections.content:
TN3270E is a Telnet option with code 40. Either side may refuse it with WON'T or DON'T, in which case traditional tn3270 can be used. A client or server that can do both is expected to try TN3270E first. Agreeing to TN3270E implies Binary Transmission and End of Record in both directions. The default is that TN3270E is not used.

The order of sub-negotiation is fixed. First comes the DEVICE-TYPE, and possibly a device name. Only then can the sides negotiate FUNCTIONS. Only after both succeed can 3270 data flow. Normally the server sends the DO TN3270E and the client answers WILL or WON'T.
sections.eli5: It is like a phone call with steps. First say hello and agree to use this special way of talking. Then say which device you are. Then pick extra features. Then talk.

sections.title: Device Types, Names and Pools
sections.content:
The server sends SEND DEVICE-TYPE. The client replies with DEVICE-TYPE REQUEST and a device type in upper-case NVT ASCII. Terminal types are IBM-3278-2, -3, -4 and -5, each also with an -E form, plus IBM-DYNAMIC. The one printer type is IBM-3287-1. The names only identify a terminal or printer family member and do not exclude capabilities. The -E forms and IBM-DYNAMIC are for clients willing to support part of the 3270 extended data stream.

The request may add CONNECT <resource-name> or ASSOCIATE <device-name>, but not both. A device-name (also called LU name or network name) names one terminal or printer. A resource-name may be a device-name or the name of a pool of devices. Both should not exceed 8 bytes. A request with neither command is a generic session request.

With CONNECT, the client asks for a specific device or any device in a pool. With ASSOCIATE, only for a printer type, the client names a terminal it was given earlier and asks for the printer paired with it. The server must accept or deny the request as a whole. It accepts with DEVICE-TYPE IS ... CONNECT <device-name>, or denies with DEVICE-TYPE REJECT REASON and a reason code. The client should use the reason code to avoid repeated failures, and either side can bail out by sending WON'T or DON'T TN3270E.
sections.eli5: The client says what kind of screen or printer it wants and, if it likes, a name. The server says yes with the name it gives, or no with a reason. A client can ask for "the printer that goes with my screen."

sections.title: Functions Negotiation
sections.content:
After device-type negotiation, the client sends FUNCTIONS REQUEST with a list of functions it wants. Functions not in the list are unsupported. The other side accepts by sending FUNCTIONS IS with exactly the same list. It rejects by sending a FUNCTIONS REQUEST whose list differs by at least one function. To avoid endless loops, neither party may re-add a function it added earlier that the other side removed. If an impasse is reached, the offended party ends negotiation with DON'T or WON'T TN3270E.

Five functions exist:

  • SCS-CTL-CODES: SNA Character Stream control codes, printer sessions only.
  • DATA-STREAM-CTL: the standard 3270 data stream, printer sessions only.
  • RESPONSES: positive and negative response handling.
  • BIND-IMAGE: lets the server send the SNA Bind image and Unbind notice.
  • SYSREQ: emulates some or all of the SYSREQ key.

A null list is allowed and is called basic TN3270E, which is for terminal sessions only. A printer session must agree to SCS-CTL-CODES, DATA-STREAM-CTL, or both.
sections.eli5: Both sides swap a list of extra features they want. They keep trimming the list until both say "that works."

sections.title: Data Messages and the Header
sections.content:
Every 3270 message is prefixed by a five-byte header and ends with Telnet IAC EOR, so a data message is <header><data><IAC EOR>. Some message types have no data. A data byte of decimal 255 must be doubled. Other Telnet commands should be sent between data messages, not inside them.

The header holds DATA-TYPE (1 byte), REQUEST-FLAG (1 byte), RESPONSE-FLAG (1 byte) and SEQ-NUMBER (2 bytes). DATA-TYPE says how to read the data. For 3270-DATA and SCS-DATA, RESPONSE-FLAG says whether a reply is expected: NO-RESPONSE (0x00), ERROR-RESPONSE (0x01) or ALWAYS-RESPONSE (0x02). In a RESPONSE message it is POSITIVE-RESPONSE (0x00) or NEGATIVE-RESPONSE (0x01). SEQ-NUMBER is used only when RESPONSES was agreed. It is sent in big endian order, with a 0xff byte doubled, and is otherwise 0x0000.

Basic TN3270E needs only the 3270-DATA and NVT-DATA types. The REQUEST-FLAG, RESPONSE-FLAG and SEQ-NUMBER fields are not used there.
sections.eli5: Each message gets a small label on the front saying what is inside and whether the sender wants a thank-you note back.

sections.title: Modes, Responses and Special Keys
sections.content:
A connection is in 3270 mode or NVT mode, starting in 3270 mode. Sending the other data type asks to switch, and a switch makes the client do the equivalent of a 3270 Erase/Reset. A server can use NVT data to show a plain menu of applications before connecting the client to one.

With RESPONSES, a sender counts its 3270-DATA and SCS-DATA messages from zero, wrapping at 32767, and puts the count in SEQ-NUMBER. The receiver sends a RESPONSE copying that number when the flag requires it. A negative response carries a one-byte detail, such as 0x01 for printer not ready. After a printer error is fixed, the client sends a REQUEST message with ERR-COND-CLEARED so the host can resume printing. A server sends PRINT-EOJ at the end of each print job.

With BIND-IMAGE, the server sends the Bind image exactly as received once the SNA session starts, and an UNBIND message when it ends.

The ATTN key is carried as the Telnet Interrupt Process command, which an SNA server passes on as a SIGNAL RU. A non-SNA server ignores it. With SYSREQ, a client sends Telnet Abort Output, and the server enters a suspended mode in which data uses SSCP-LU-DATA. A server that cannot send USS commands accepts only LOGOFF and otherwise answers COMMAND UNRECOGNIZED. Pressing SYSREQ again resumes the session.
sections.eli5: Messages can be numbered so the other side can say "got number 7, all good" or "number 7 broke." Special keys like ATTN are sent as Telnet signals that the server translates for the mainframe.

sections.title: Structured Fields and Implementation Notes
sections.content:
A client that negotiates an -E terminal type, IBM-DYNAMIC or a printer type must answer the Read Partition Query (Type 02) and all forms of the Read Partition Query List (Type 03). The reply, a Query Reply, tells host applications which structured field functions and other capabilities, such as extended color, the device supports.

Keep-alives are optional. The RFC names three methods: TCP Keepalive, Telnet IAC NOP and the Telnet DO TIMING-MARK option. Implementations that support keep-alives are recommended to support all three, and both sides should always answer TIMING-MARKs. The RFC also gives worked examples, such as a generic pool terminal session, a request for a specific name, and a printer session set up with ASSOCIATE.
sections.eli5: Clients that do fancy things must be able to answer "what can you do?" Programs can also send little pings to find out whether the other side is still there.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: TN3270E adds no security features beyond ordinary Telnet, so a TN3270E session is no more secure than an ordinary Telnet session. Once standard Telnet authentication or privacy mechanisms are defined, they may also work with TN3270E. The RFC singles out one use of authentication: deciding whether a given user may use a specific terminal or printer device-name.
sections.eli5: This memo does not add locks. It is as safe, or unsafe, as plain Telnet.

messages.note: The 3270 data stream can now be exchanged.

fields.name: DATA-TYPE
fields.desc: How the data portion is to be interpreted.

fields.name: REQUEST-FLAG
fields.desc: Meaningful only when DATA-TYPE is REQUEST.

fields.name: RESPONSE-FLAG
fields.desc: Whether a response is expected, or the response itself.

fields.name: SEQ-NUMBER
fields.desc: Matches responses to data messages when RESPONSES is agreed.

items.label: RESPONSE
items.desc: Device-status information; RESPONSE-FLAG gives positive or negative.

items.label: NVT-DATA
items.desc: Data to be read as NVT data.

items.label: PRINT-EOJ
items.desc: No data; server only, printer sessions only.
